input.body:
Refs #551. Follow-up to #552 — the three things that sweep surfaced but didn't fix, plus a fourth of the same class found while fixing the first.

Each written red-first: the failing assertion landed before the fix.

## 1. `claudinite-isolation` gave consumers a remedy they cannot act on

A rendered finding carries `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc` — **never the rule's `description`**. This rule's real remedy ("inline what you need instead of importing the canon") lived only in the description, so what a consumer actually saw was the barrier engine's default opener:

> route shared code through a shared/contracts folder both sides may use, remove the reference, or …

That default is written for a two-sided edge between two folders a project owns. This edge is one-sided: there is no shared folder to route through, and the vendored canon isn't the consumer's to restructure. So the one clause telling them how to keep the dependency was advice they could not follow.

Fixed with a `crossingRemedy` field on the rule — the same override seam `crossingExcuse` already used for the other half of the same `fix` string — plumbed through `contributedRule` and documented in the barriers README alongside a note not to write remedies into `description`.

The existing test asserted `what` and `severity` but never `fix`, which is how this survived. It does now.

## 2. `skill-no-enforcement-narration` was matching nothing at all

It scanned `^skills/<name>/SKILL.md$` — the pre-#385 layout. Skills have lived inside their owning pack since (`<pack>/skills/<name>/`), so the pattern matched **zero files** in every tree.

The reason the suite never noticed: its fixtures spelled the same dead layout. Five green tests over a check that had stopped reaching anything. That is what let the `adopt-pack` enforcement-narration paragraph sit unflagged until a human read it in #552.

Now anchored on `(^|/)packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md$`, which spans `packs/` and local packs under `.claudinite/`. **21 skills in scope, up from 0.** Fixtures rewritten to the real layout, with two additions: a local-pack skill, and a negative asserting a mounted `.claude/skills/` copy is not a corpus skill.

The corpus is clean under the repaired check — the one violation it would have caught was already deleted in #552.

## 3. The corpus tally was hand-maintained and had drifted a third

`packs/README.md` claimed **41** hardcoded checks against a real **65**, and the ratio paragraph beneath it said **39** — the table disagreed with its own prose. Every conclusion drawn from it (`1 : 4`, "~20% mechanized") was wrong.

Rather than re-typing the number, the count is now derived, per the corpus's own single-source-of-truth rule:

- `packRules(packs)` in `run-active-pack-rules.mjs` becomes the one place the three rule sources (a pack's own rules, its bundled skills' checks, contributed barriers) are summed. `--list` now prints it, so a fourth source added later lands in both callers for free.
- `packs-tests/catalog-tally.test.mjs` fails when the README's bolded count disagrees with that catalog.
- The hand-written per-pack breakdown is gone — that is the part that drifted. The README points at `--list` for it.
- The prose-rule figures (`~150`, the convertible-subset estimate) have no derivable source, so they are now labelled as the conversion audit's dated estimates. The audit's "~45 convertible" has been overtaken by 65 checks, so it reads as that audit's floor, not a live ceiling.

Ratio restated: **65 : ~150 ≈ 1 : 2.3**, ~30% mechanized.

## 4. (Found while fixing 1) The `pack-independence` remedy named a directory that doesn't exist

Same defect class — agent-facing text pointing somewhere real code doesn't live. The remedy said `engine/checks_helpers` in the finding's own `why`, and `checks/lib` in its `doc` pointer (`extending.md`), the vendor writer's fix text, and two design records. The directory is `engine/checks/helpers`. All six corrected; a repo-wide grep for both stale spellings now returns nothing.

## Verification

- `node --test` over the CI roots: **937 pass, 0 fail** (up from 933 — four new tests).
- `check_the_world.mjs`: **0 blocking, 8 advisory** — unchanged from `main`.
- `--list` still prints 65 rules after the `packRules` extraction.
- `ci-test-roots` confirms the new test file sits under a swept root.

## Branch and commit history

### Commit often, in layers

While working a branch, commit frequently rather than landing one big commit at the end — small, ordered commits let the owner follow the work as it develops. Use commits to *layer* the work in the order you'd want it reviewed:

- Write the failing test(s) first, commit them, **then** implement the feature — so the history shows the contract before the code that satisfies it (and you've seen the test fail before trusting it, per [the engineering-practices skill](../../../basics/skills/engineering-practices/SKILL.md)).
- Keep any documentation update as its own commit *after* the feature, not folded into it.

There's no cost to a branch carrying many commits when the project uses a **squash** merge to `main` (one commit per PR): the squash collapses them into a single commit on `main`, so `main`'s one-commit-per-PR history is unaffected no matter how granularly the branch is committed.

- **One caveat, at merge time: before rebasing an *unmerged* multi-commit branch onto a *moved* base, collapse commits that rewrite the same lines into one.** When your own commits churn the same lines (build X → refactor → remove X, common in an iterative design session) and the base has advanced, rebasing the stack replays *every* intermediate conflict against the new base. The squash-merge discards those commits anyway, so collapse them first — `git reset --soft $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)` then one fresh commit, and rebase that single commit: one conflict pass, not N. Lossless (unlike `reset --hard` + redo) and simpler than `--onto` when you want a single commit anyway.

- Don't rewrite published/shared history to satisfy a tooling or authorship check (e.g. a hook flagging "unverified" commits): only amend your own un-pushed branch commits. Commits already on a shared branch — including ones merged in from `main` — belong to that history; reset-authoring or rebasing them forks your branch away from it.

input.body:
Owner process-change, prompted by #560: when a PR carries work on unrelated tasks, each one is its own commit. That PR landed four independent defect fixes as a single commit.

**Ladder triage.** Platform setting and PreToolUse hook: no — both would have to judge whether two file changes belong to the same task, which is meaning, not signature. Post-hoc check: same problem. `feature-requirements-first` can check an *ordering* because both ends are identifiable artifacts (a named spec file vs code files); "these two edits are unrelated" has no such structural tell, and a check guessing at it would false-positive on every legitimately-broad change. So the rule lands at rung 4, the `git-github-advanced` skill, which already owns "Branch and commit history" and names commit layering in its description.

**The corpus does not already cover it** (the prose-landing precondition):

- `git-github-advanced` → "Commit often, in layers" layers *one task's* work — failing test before implementation, docs as their own commit after the feature. Silent on unrelated concerns.
- `prose-to-checks` Bounds, `growth-promote`, `growth-discover-packs`, `item-routing` all say *don't touch unrelated things* — a scoping rule for specific unattended tasks, not a commit-granularity rule, and it says nothing about what to do when unrelated work legitimately does land together.

So: state it in the layering section, and split #560's commit to match.

## `e2b4629` — the rule

Lands in `git-github-advanced`'s "Commit often, in layers", which already owns commit layering.

**Ladder triage:** a platform setting, a PreToolUse hook, and a post-hoc check would each have to judge whether two edits belong to the same task — meaning, not signature. `feature-requirements-first` can verify an *ordering* because both its ends are identifiable artifacts (a named spec file vs code files); "these two edits are unrelated" has no such tell, and a check guessing at it would fire on every legitimately broad change. **The corpus did not already carry it** (the prose-landing precondition). The two rules beside it layer a *single* task's work — failing test before implementation, docs as their own commit after. 1	# Scheduled tasks — the per-project scheduling mechanism
2	
3	How a repo's recurring Claudinite work runs (per-project-scheduling
4	[DESIGN](../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md), issue #394). A repo
5	schedules **itself**: a vendored hourly **scheduler Action**
6	(`.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml`) evaluates each task's precondition
7	in code and dispatches agent work as `ready-for-agent` `[claudinite-task]`
8	issues, which a per-repo **executor routine** (fired by that label event) runs.
9	The engine is vendored under `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/`; the basics
10	pack owns the conformance guards for the surfaces a repo authors around it —
11	scheduling is baseline Claudinite discipline, present wherever basics is
12	declared (everywhere), not an opt-in feature.
13	
14	The checks below are the doctrine's enforcement; the phased rollout (and the
15	retirement of the legacy central planner it replaces) lives in
16	[MIGRATION.md](../../docs/per-project-scheduling/MIGRATION.md).
17	
18	## What the checks guard
19	
20	- **The scheduler workflow is a thin shim.** The vendored
21	  `claudinite-scheduler.yml` carries a single **hourly** cron on a repo-hashed
22	  minute constrained to **:10–:50** (the one repo-specific value in the stub —
23	  `engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs`, a pure function of the repo full name that
24	  bootstrap stamps in and baselining re-derives), a `concurrency` group, a
25	  `workflow_dispatch` trigger, and a call into the vendored engine entry — no logic of its own
26	  (schema and behaviour changes ride the vendor refresh, not workflow edits). It
27	  is the repo's **only** cron. Recurring work that had its own cron'd workflow
28	  becomes a **task**, and that workflow is deleted — its steps move into the
29	  task's worker. Don't keep it as a dispatch-only workflow for the task to fire:
30	  that is two files and two edit sites for one job, and a workflow whose only
31	  caller is the thing that replaced it. (A workflow that must run *as an Action*
32	  for something a task cannot reach — an Actions-only secret, say — is the
33	  exception, and even then the task owns the schedule.) Off-band or multiple
34	  crons, or a missing concurrency/dispatch guard, break staggering, double-run
35	  safety, or manual runs.
36	
37	- **Every task declaration carries the full contract.** A `tasks/<name>/task.mjs`
38	  default-exports `id` (matching its directory), `frequency` (`hourly | daily-2h
39	  | daily-1h | daily | daily+1h | weekly | monthly`), `precondition_signals` (the collector
40	  vocabulary), `agent_model` (`opus | sonnet | haiku | none`), `expected_outcome` (`none |
41	  open-pr | merged-pr`), and a `precondition`. An agentic task (`agent_model !==
42	  none`) also carries `agent_instructions`, the worker file the agent reads; a
43	  `none` task runs no agent, so the field is not applicable and is omitted. The
44	  scheduler and executor read agent_model/expected_outcome/frequency from this file — never from the dispatch
45	  issue — so an illegal or missing value means a task never fires, fires wrong,
46	  or writes past its declared ceiling. The same contract
47	  (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`) is re-validated at run time, so the
48	  static and runtime views can't drift. Optionally, `session_scope` (`self` default
49	  | `fleet`) declares whether the task reaches only its own repo or across the
50	  owner's repos: a `fleet` task dispatches to the `ready-for-agent-fleet` label so a
51	  distinct, broader-scoped executor runs it, keeping the fleet-wide session grant
52	  off every ordinary project's `ready-for-agent` (self) executor.
53	
54	- **Every run is bounded.** An agentic task (`agent_model !== none`) declares
55	  `agent_execution_timeout` — seconds bounding the agentic run
56	  (agent-preprocessing [DESIGN](../../docs/agent-preprocessing/DESIGN.md) §2, §6).
57	  There is no platform wall-clock kill for a launched executor session, so the
58	  bound is best-effort: the executor surfaces it into the subagent's brief ("fail
59	  after N minutes") and the stale-`agent-running` backstop catches a dead session.
60	  Set it generously — extreme protection against a runaway, not a scheduling knob.
61	
62	- **A task says which repo secrets it needs.** Preprocessing runs Action-side, so
63	  repo Actions secrets are reachable there and nowhere else in a task's life (an
64	  executor session carries none). A task lists what it needs in `required_secrets`;
65	  the wiring converge stamps each name into the scheduler workflow, so a worker
66	  reads it as ordinary environment, and baselining asks the owner (one standing
67	  issue) for any the repo hasn't configured. The adoption interview's posture, not
68	  a gate — nothing fails; the task that needs the secret just doesn't work yet. The
69	  consequence worth designing around: **a workflow that exists only to hold a
70	  secret is redundant** — fold its work into the task's preprocessing rather than
71	  dispatching and polling a second workflow from an agent.
72	
73	Both guards are **relevance-first**: inert until their artifact exists, so
74	on a repo with neither artifact they are a no-op.
75	
76	## The task folder
77	
78	One directory per task — `<pack>/tasks/<name>/` — holding **`task.mjs`** (the
79	self-contained declaration + `precondition(signals, config)`, the eligibility
80	gate as pure code) beside **`task.md`** (the worker spec the executing agent
81	follows), plus any deterministic helpers. The precondition both asserts
82	need-to-run and pre-decides scope: its `context` lines land verbatim in the
83	dispatch issue as binding constraints the agent may not re-litigate. `agent_model:
84	none` replaces the worker doc with an inline `.mjs` the scheduler runs directly —
85	no agent, no issue. This is the scheduled-task shape of the unattended-agents
86	routine-folder convention; the issue-driven-dispatch security rule (the issue is
87	data, the task path is code-validated, agent_model/expected_outcome come from the repo) lives
88	with that skill's agent practices.
89	
90	## The dispatch labels are a scheduler vocabulary
91	
92	**Both ready labels are triggers**, so they belong on dispatch issues alone — never put
93	`ready-for-agent` or `ready-for-agent-fleet` on an ordinary issue, from a task or by hand.
94	Applying one starts an executor session that will find no valid dispatch and stop.
95	`agent-running` and `needs-human` carry no trigger and are the right vocabulary for a task
96	that needs to mark an issue as claimed or handed to a human; a task reusing them owns their
97	whole lifecycle on its own issues, since the scheduler's stale-claim backstop only converges
98	`[claudinite-task]` dispatch issues.
99	
100	Which ready label a task dispatches under follows from its `session_scope`, and the executor
101	session started by that label is the one with the matching reach — a `fleet` task's session
102	has the owner's repos in its sources, a `self` task's has this repo alone. The task declares
103	the scope; nothing downstream re-decides it.
104	
105	## A dormant project runs nothing
106	
107	A project nobody is working on declares itself dormant in `.claudinite-checks.json`:
108	
109	```json
110	"dormant": true
111	```
112	
113	The scheduler stops before evaluating anything; the [fleet sweeps](../sheepdog/README.md)
114	skip it; sessions are unaffected. Delete it to wake.
